title: Definition, Scope and Importance of Statistics and Biostatistics
objectives: Define statistics and biostatistics in clear academic language.
Distinguish descriptive and inferential statistics.
Explain the role of statistics in biological research and decision-making.
Identify the limitations of statistical methods.
intro: Biological observations vary. No two organisms are exactly alike, and even repeated measurements on the same organism may differ because of natural variation, measurement error or environmental influence. Statistics provides a disciplined method for converting such observations into organised evidence. Biostatistics applies those methods to living systems, health, agriculture and environmental science.
history: The word statistics is historically linked to the study of the state. Early statistical work dealt with population counts, taxation and public administration. During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the work of Francis Galton, Karl Pearson, Ronald A. Fisher, William S. Gosset and others established modern methods of correlation, regression, experimental design and hypothesis testing. In India, statistical education and official statistics developed strongly through the work of P. C. Mahalanobis and the Indian Statistical Institute.
definition: Statistics is the science of collecting, classifying, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical or categorical data for description, comparison, inference and decision-making. Biostatistics is the application of statistical principles and methods to biology, medicine, public health, agriculture, fisheries and allied life sciences.
need: Biological systems show natural variation.
Large datasets cannot be understood by inspection alone.
Samples must be used to infer population characteristics.
Scientific claims require estimates of uncertainty.
Research results must be communicated through tables, diagrams and numerical summaries.

classification.name: Descriptive statistics
classification.text: Methods used to organise, summarise and present observed data, such as tables, graphs, mean and standard deviation.

classification.name: Inferential statistics
classification.text: Methods used to estimate population characteristics or test hypotheses from sample data.

classification.name: Parametric methods
classification.text: Methods based on assumptions about population parameters or distributional form.

classification.name: Non-parametric methods
classification.text: Methods requiring fewer distributional assumptions, often based on ranks or frequencies.

explanation: A statistical investigation normally begins with a clearly stated objective. The investigator defines the population, identifies variables, chooses a sampling or experimental design, collects data, checks quality, summarises observations and finally draws conclusions. Each stage affects the validity of the next.

Statistics does not replace biological reasoning. It supports reasoning by making variation, uncertainty and evidence explicit. A statistically significant result may be biologically trivial, while an important biological effect may fail to reach significance in a small study.

Zoology: Comparing body measurements among animal populations.
Estimating abundance from quadrats, transects or capture–recapture studies.
Botany: Comparing germination or growth under treatments.
Biotechnology: Analysing PCR, ELISA and fermentation data.
Microbiology: Comparing colony counts and antimicrobial responses.
Medicine: Clinical trials, disease surveillance and diagnostic evaluation.
Agriculture: Crop yield trials and varietal comparisons.

limitations: Conclusions depend on data quality and design.
Averages may conceal important subgroups.
Association does not establish causation.
Incorrect assumptions or test selection can mislead.
Statistical significance is not identical to practical importance.
precautions: Define the research question before collecting data.
Use appropriate sampling and measurement methods.
Retain raw data and document cleaning decisions.
Report assumptions, uncertainty and limitations.
Avoid selective reporting of favourable results.

examples.q: Five fish have lengths 12, 13, 15, 15 and 20 cm. What can statistics do?
steps: Calculate a typical value such as the mean or median.
Describe spread and identify the unusually long fish.
Compare the sample with another fish population if available.
examples.answer: Statistics converts the five measurements into interpretable summaries and comparisons.

examples.q: Two ponds have the same mean fish length but different standard deviations. What does this imply?
steps: The means indicate similar central size.
The pond with larger SD has greater variation in fish length.
Management interpretation should consider both centre and spread.
examples.answer: Equal means do not imply equal biological uniformity.

examples.q: Explain why a statistically significant treatment effect may not be biologically important.
steps: Statistical significance depends on effect size, variability and sample size.
A very small effect may produce a low p-value in a very large sample.
Biological importance depends on magnitude, cost, survival, health or ecological relevance.
examples.answer: A complete conclusion reports effect magnitude and uncertainty, not only p-value.

misconceptions: Statistics is only the calculation of averages.
A large sample automatically corrects biased sampling.
A low p-value proves the research hypothesis.
exam: Begin with an exact definition.
Write the stages of a statistical investigation.
Give at least four biological applications.
Mention limitations to obtain a complete long-answer response.
mnemonic: C-C-P-A-I: Collect, Classify, Present, Analyse, Interpret.
summary: Statistics organises data and supports inference.
Biostatistics applies statistical reasoning to living systems.
Good design and valid measurement are more fundamental than calculation.
selfcheck: Give two zoological applications of biostatistics.
references: Agarwal, B. L. Basic Statistics. New Age International Publishers, New Delhi.
Gupta, S. P. Statistical Methods. Sultan Chand & Sons, New Delhi.
Snedecor, G. W., and Cochran, W. G. Statistical Methods. Iowa State University Press, Ames.

title: Population, Sample, Census, Parameter and Statistic
objectives: Distinguish population and sample.
Define census, sampling unit, sampling frame, parameter and statistic.
Explain target and accessible populations.
Evaluate whether a sample is representative.
intro: Most biological populations are too large, dispersed, inaccessible or costly to study completely. Investigators therefore observe a sample and use sample statistics to learn about population parameters. The quality of this inference depends on how clearly the population is defined and how the sample is selected.
definition: A population is the complete set of units about which a conclusion is intended. A sample is a subset of those units actually observed. A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population; a statistic is a numerical characteristic computed from a sample.
need: To make large investigations feasible.
To reduce time, cost and destructive testing.
To estimate population characteristics.
To quantify sampling uncertainty.

classification.name: Target population
classification.text: The full population to which the researcher wishes to generalise.

classification.name: Accessible population
classification.text: The portion that can realistically be reached.

classification.name: Finite population
classification.text: A population with a countable number of units.

classification.name: Infinite or conceptual population
classification.text: A theoretically unlimited set of possible observations.

explanation: A sampling unit is the basic unit selected, such as an individual fish, household, quadrat or school. The observational unit is the unit on which measurements are made; it may or may not be identical to the sampling unit.

A sampling frame is the operational list or map from which a sample is selected. A frame that excludes some eligible units creates undercoverage. A frame containing duplicates can give some units a higher chance of selection.
A census observes every unit. It may be appropriate for small populations, but it can still contain non-sampling errors such as incorrect measurement, missing records or poor definitions.

Zoology: Target population: all house sparrows in a district; sample: birds counted at selected sites.
Botany: All trees in a forest reserve versus trees within sampled quadrats.
Biotechnology: All production batches versus quality-control samples.
Microbiology: All bacterial colonies on plates versus colonies selected for identification.
Medicine: All patients with a condition versus recruited patients.
Agriculture: All farms in a block versus sampled farms.
Fisheries: All fish in a reservoir versus a netted sample.
Environmental science: All water points versus monitored stations.

advantages: Can produce high-quality estimates with a probability design.
limitations: Sampling error is unavoidable.
Coverage and non-response can create bias.
Rare subgroups may be missed.
A convenience sample may not support population inference.
precautions: Define place, time and eligibility.
Distinguish target from accessible population.
Use an up-to-date sampling frame.
Document exclusions and non-response.

examples.q: A college has 1,200 students; 120 are surveyed. Identify population and sample.
examples.answer: The conclusion can be generalised only if selection and response are appropriate.

examples.q: A fish survey samples only near the landing site. Is it representative of the lake?
steps: The accessible area differs from the target lake.
Fish distribution may vary by depth and habitat.
The sample has spatial selection bias.
examples.answer: No; a stratified or spatially distributed design is needed.

examples.q: Explain parameter and statistic with symbols.
steps: Population mean is μ, population SD is σ, population proportion is P.
Sample mean is x̄, sample SD is s, sample proportion is p̂.
Statistics estimate parameters and vary from sample to sample.
examples.answer: A parameter is fixed but usually unknown; a statistic is observable but subject to sampling variation.

misconceptions: Population always means people.
A census is always error-free.
A sample is representative merely because it is large.
exam: Use biological examples.
Include symbols μ, σ, x̄ and s.
Explain representativeness rather than merely defining sample.
mnemonic: P is Population and Parameter; S is Sample and Statistic.
summary: Population defines the scope of inference.
Sample quality depends on selection, coverage and response.
Statistics are used to estimate parameters.
selfcheck: Why can a census contain error?
Give one example where destructive sampling is necessary.
references: Gupta, S. P. Statistical Methods. Sultan Chand & Sons, New Delhi.
Kothari, C. R. Research Methodology: Methods and Techniques. New Age International Publishers, New Delhi.

title: Types of Variables and Scales of Measurement
objectives: Classify qualitative and quantitative variables.
Distinguish discrete and continuous data.
Explain nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales.
Identify dependent, independent and confounding variables.
intro: Correct statistical analysis begins with correct identification of variables. The same biological characteristic may be recorded in different ways: age may be measured in years, grouped into age classes or reduced to adult and juvenile categories. Each representation permits different summaries and tests.
definition: A variable is a characteristic that can take different values among units or across occasions. A constant does not vary within the defined context.
need: Choice of graph depends on variable type.
Choice of average and dispersion depends on measurement scale.
Statistical tests require particular data structures.
Coding and interpretation depend on clear definitions.

classification.name: Qualitative / categorical
classification.text: Values are categories, such as species or blood group.

classification.name: Quantitative / numerical
classification.text: Values represent counts or measurements.

classification.name: Discrete
classification.text: Countable values, commonly integers, such as number of offspring.

classification.name: Continuous
classification.text: Measurements that may take any value within a range, such as body mass.

explanation: Nominal data have categories without inherent order. Ordinal data have meaningful order, but differences between categories are not necessarily equal. Interval data have equal intervals but no true zero. Ratio data have equal intervals and a meaningful zero.

An independent variable is manipulated or treated as a predictor. A dependent variable is the measured response. A confounder is related to both and may create or obscure an apparent association. A control variable is deliberately held constant or adjusted for.

Binary variables have two categories. Count variables are discrete quantitative variables and may have skewed distributions. Time-to-event variables include both event time and censoring information and require specialised methods beyond the present syllabus.

Zoology: Species = nominal; maturity stage = ordinal; egg count = discrete; body length = continuous.
Botany: Leaf colour = nominal; disease grade = ordinal; leaf number = discrete; plant height = continuous.
Biotechnology: Treatment group = nominal; expression intensity category = ordinal; colony number = discrete; DNA concentration = continuous.
Microbiology: Organism identity, resistance grade, CFU count and inhibition-zone diameter.
Medicine: Blood group, pain grade, number of attacks and blood pressure.
Agriculture: Variety, quality grade, fruit count and yield.
Fisheries: Species, gonadal stage, catch count and weight.
Environmental science: Habitat type, pollution class, species count and dissolved oxygen.

advantages: Measurement scale clarifies permissible mathematical operations.
limitations: Categories can oversimplify continuous variation.
Poorly defined variables reduce reproducibility.
Ordinal scores are often incorrectly treated as interval measurements.
precautions: State operational definitions and units.
Use mutually exclusive categories.
Do not encode missing values as a valid category unless explicitly labelled.
Preserve continuous measurements before creating groups.

examples.q: Classify blood group, number of eggs and fish weight.
examples.answer: The three variables require different summaries and graphs.

examples.q: Disease severity is coded 1, 2 and 3. Is the difference between 1 and 2 equal to 2 and 3?
steps: Equal numerical spacing is not guaranteed.
examples.answer: It is ordinal, not automatically interval.

examples.q: A study examines feed type and fish growth, but water temperature differs among tanks. Identify variables.
steps: Tank may be the experimental unit.
examples.answer: Temperature must be controlled, randomised or adjusted.

misconceptions: Any variable written with numbers is quantitative.
Ordinal categories have equal intervals.
Dependent variable means a variable that is unimportant.
exam: Use a four-column table with definition, property and example.
Explain why scale affects analysis.
Include independent and dependent variables.
mnemonic: NOIR: Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio.
summary: Variables may be categorical or quantitative.
Measurement scales determine valid operations.
Operational definitions are essential for reproducibility.
selfcheck: Why is pH usually treated as an interval-like measure rather than a ratio scale?
Why should continuous data not be grouped too early?
references: Gupta, S. C., and Kapoor, V. K. Fundamentals of Applied Statistics. Sultan Chand & Sons, New Delhi.

title: Collection and Sources of Data: Primary and Secondary Data
objectives: Differentiate primary and secondary data.
Describe observation, experiment, interview and questionnaire methods.
Evaluate secondary data quality.
Explain data-editing and ethical precautions.
intro: Data quality begins at collection. A sophisticated analysis cannot correct unclear measurements, biased questions or incompatible secondary sources. The investigator must therefore choose a collection method that fits the research objective and produces valid, reliable and ethical evidence.
definition: Primary data are collected first-hand for the current study. Secondary data were collected previously for another purpose or as part of an existing information system and are reused in the present study.
need: To match data source to research purpose.
To assess cost, time and reliability.
To plan quality control and ethical safeguards.

classification.name: Observation
classification.text: Systematic recording of events, behaviour or conditions.

classification.name: Experiment
classification.text: Deliberate manipulation of one or more factors under controlled conditions.

classification.name: Interview
classification.text: Questions administered by an investigator.

classification.name: Questionnaire / schedule
classification.text: Structured items completed by respondents or enumerators.

classification.name: Records and databases
classification.text: Administrative, laboratory, census or published sources.

explanation: Primary data offer control over definitions, units and quality procedures, but require resources and ethical approval. Secondary data are economical and may cover large populations or long periods, but the investigator has limited control over original design.

Reliability refers to consistency of measurement; validity refers to whether the method measures the intended concept. Calibration, training, pilot testing, duplicate measurement and standard operating procedures improve quality.
A data dictionary or codebook should define every variable, unit, code and missing-value convention. Raw data should be preserved separately from cleaned data.

Zoology: Field observations of bird behaviour; museum records as secondary data.
Biotechnology: New spectrophotometric readings; archived sequencing datasets.
Microbiology: Fresh culture counts; hospital antibiogram records.
Environmental science: New water samples; long-term monitoring databases.

advantages: Primary data are tailored to the question.
Secondary data save time and may enable historical comparison.
limitations: Primary collection can be expensive and slow.
Secondary definitions may not match current needs.
Missingness and changes in measurement can limit comparability.
precautions: Pilot test instruments.
Train observers.
Use calibrated equipment.
Check consent and confidentiality.
Evaluate authority, date, methods and completeness of secondary sources.

examples.q: Classify a student survey and a census report.
steps: Student survey collected for the study = primary.
examples.answer: Classification depends on relation to the present investigation.

examples.q: Two hospitals use different definitions of infection. Can their rates be directly combined?
steps: The numerator and denominator may differ.
Harmonisation or separate analysis is required.
examples.answer: Do not combine without methodological reconciliation.

examples.q: Prepare a quality checklist for secondary ecological data.
examples.answer: Secondary data must be audited before analysis.

misconceptions: Published data are automatically accurate.
Primary data are always superior.
Reliability and validity mean the same thing.
exam: Write definitions first.
Use a comparison table.
Add merits, demerits and quality checks.
mnemonic: A-D-M-C: Authority, Definitions, Method, Completeness.
summary: Source choice affects validity and feasibility.
Primary and secondary data have complementary roles.
Quality assurance must be planned before analysis.
selfcheck: List five checks for secondary data.
Why is a pilot study useful?
references: Kothari, C. R. Research Methodology: Methods and Techniques. New Age International Publishers, New Delhi.

title: Sampling Methods and Sampling Procedure
objectives: Classify probability and non-probability sampling.
Explain simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster and multistage sampling.
Describe sampling procedure step by step.
Identify sampling and non-sampling errors.
intro: Sampling is not merely taking a convenient subset. It is a planned procedure linking a population to the observations collected. Probability sampling assigns known selection probabilities and supports estimation of sampling error. Non-probability methods may be practical for exploration but generally provide weaker population inference.
definition: Sampling is the process of selecting units from a population so that observations on the selected units can be used to describe or infer characteristics of the population.
need: A census may be impossible or destructive.
Sampling reduces cost and time.
Careful sampling can improve measurement quality.
Probability designs permit estimation of uncertainty.

classification.name: Simple random sampling
classification.text: Every unit and every sample of a given size has a known equal chance under the design.

classification.name: Systematic sampling
classification.text: Select a random start and then every kth unit.

classification.name: Stratified sampling
classification.text: Divide population into strata and sample within each stratum.

classification.name: Cluster sampling
classification.text: Select natural groups such as villages, schools or sampling sites.

classification.name: Multistage sampling
classification.text: Select progressively at two or more levels.

classification.name: Non-probability sampling
classification.text: Convenience, purposive, quota and snowball methods without known selection probabilities.

explanation: In simple random sampling, units may be selected by lottery or computer-generated random numbers. Replacement means a selected unit can be selected again; most biological surveys use sampling without replacement.
For systematic sampling, the interval k is approximately N/n. A random start between 1 and k is chosen. Periodic ordering can produce bias if the period matches k.

Stratification is useful when subgroups differ but are internally more homogeneous. Allocation may be proportionate or disproportionate. Disproportionate designs require weights for population estimates.
Cluster sampling is economical for dispersed populations, but units within a cluster are often correlated, reducing effective sample information.

Sampling error arises because only a subset is observed. Non-sampling errors include undercoverage, non-response, measurement error, data-entry error and interviewer bias. Increasing sample size reduces random sampling error but does not automatically remove systematic bias.

Zoology: Stratify a forest by habitat before sampling butterflies.
Use systematic transect points for intertidal organisms.
Microbiology: Systematic selection of specimens from a laboratory log.
Environmental science: Multistage selection of districts, villages and water points.

advantages: Cluster and multistage designs reduce field cost.
limitations: Complete frames may be unavailable.
Complex designs require weights and specialised variance estimation.
Non-response can undermine representativeness.
precautions: State inclusion criteria.
Avoid convenience substitution for non-responders.
Record selection probabilities.
Document departures from protocol.
Use randomisation transparently.

examples.q: N = 1,000 and n = 100. Find the systematic interval.
steps: Choose a random start from 1 to 10 and then every 10th unit.
examples.answer: Sampling interval k = 10.

examples.q: A lake has shallow, medium and deep zones. Which sampling method is suitable?
steps: Fish communities may differ by depth.
examples.answer: Stratified random sampling.

examples.q: Explain why cluster sampling often has lower precision than simple random sampling of the same number of units.
steps: Units within a cluster share environment or behaviour.
The effective independent information is less than the nominal sample size.
examples.answer: Clustering introduces a design effect that can increase variance.

misconceptions: Systematic sampling is random even without a random start.
Cluster sampling and stratified sampling are the same.
A larger convenience sample becomes a probability sample.
exam: Draw a classification chart.
Give procedure, merit, limitation and example for each method.
State k = N/n for systematic sampling.
mnemonic: R-S-S-C-M: Random, Systematic, Stratified, Cluster, Multistage.
summary: Sampling design determines the strength of inference.
Probability methods use known selection mechanisms.
Bias is not cured merely by increasing sample size.

formulae.name: Systematic sampling interval
formulae.meaning: Approximate spacing between selected units.
formulae.use: Systematic selection after a random start.
formulae.avoid: When ordering has a cycle matching k.
formulae.bio: Selecting every 10th fish record after a random start.

selfcheck: Why may survey weights be needed?
references: Cochran, W. G. Sampling Techniques. Wiley, New York.
Kothari, C. R. Research Methodology: Methods and Techniques. New Age International Publishers, New Delhi.

title: Classification, Frequency Distribution and Tabulation
objectives: Construct discrete and grouped frequency distributions.
Explain class limits, boundaries, width and midpoint.
Calculate relative and cumulative frequencies.
Describe parts and types of statistical tables.
intro: Raw data are often difficult to interpret. Classification groups observations according to shared characteristics. A frequency distribution reveals how often values or intervals occur, while tabulation arranges data in rows and columns for comparison.
definition: A frequency distribution is an organised presentation of distinct values or class intervals together with the number of observations in each. Tabulation is the systematic presentation of data in rows and columns.
need: To condense raw observations.
To reveal concentration, spread and shape.
To prepare data for graphs and statistical calculation.
To support comparison across groups.

classification.name: Qualitative classification
classification.text: Grouping by attributes such as sex, species or habitat.

classification.name: Quantitative classification
classification.text: Grouping by numerical values or intervals.

classification.name: Chronological classification
classification.text: Arrangement by time.

classification.name: Geographical classification
classification.text: Arrangement by place.

classification.name: Discrete frequency distribution
classification.text: Frequency for each countable value.

classification.name: Continuous grouped distribution
classification.text: Frequency within class intervals.

explanation: Class limits are the stated lowest and highest values in a class. Class boundaries are the true dividing points between adjacent continuous classes. Class width is the difference between boundaries. Class midpoint is the average of the limits or boundaries.

Inclusive classes such as 10–19 and 20–29 are common for rounded or discrete data. They can be converted to continuous boundaries 9.5–19.5 and 19.5–29.5 when measurements are recorded to the nearest unit. Exclusive classes such as 10–20 and 20–30 already meet at a boundary.
Relative frequency is f/N. Percentage frequency is 100f/N. Less-than cumulative frequency accumulates upward; more-than cumulative frequency accumulates downward.

A complete table contains table number, title, headnote, captions, stubs, body, footnote and source. Simple, two-way, three-way and manifold tables classify data by increasing numbers of characteristics.

Zoology: Frequency distribution of fish lengths or parasite counts.
Microbiology: Colony-count distribution.
Fisheries: Catch-frequency table by species and season.

limitations: Grouping loses exact individual values.
Poor class choices can conceal patterns.
Open-ended classes limit some calculations.
precautions: Classes must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
Avoid too many or too few classes.
Use consistent width unless unequal width is necessary and clearly handled.
State units and source.

examples.q: For values 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, construct a discrete frequency table.
examples.answer: The mode is visible as value 3.

examples.q: Convert inclusive classes 10–19 and 20–29 to boundaries.
examples.answer: The classes become continuous.

examples.q: Explain construction of a grouped distribution from 50 observations.
examples.answer: The final table should state class interval, tally, frequency and optional cumulative measures.

misconceptions: Class limits and boundaries are identical in all cases.
The number of classes is fixed by a universal rule.
A blank table cell means zero.
exam: Draw a model statistical table.
Define every class term.
Show boundary conversion with calculation.
mnemonic: NT-HC-BFS: Number, Title, Headnote, Captions, Body, Footnote, Source.
summary: Classification organises data.
Frequency distributions support graphs and calculations.
Good tables are complete, clear and comparable.

formulae.name: Relative frequency
formulae.meaning: Proportion of observations in a value or class.
formulae.use: Comparing distributions with different totals.
formulae.avoid: Do not confuse with cumulative frequency.
formulae.bio: Proportion of fish in a length class.

formulae.name: Class midpoint
formulae.meaning: Representative central value of a class.
assumptions: Values are treated as distributed around the midpoint
formulae.use: Grouped mean calculation.
formulae.avoid: Do not treat midpoint as every actual observation.
formulae.bio: Representative length for a fish-size class.

selfcheck: Construct a less-than cumulative frequency column.
references: Gupta, S. P. Statistical Methods. Sultan Chand & Sons, New Delhi.

title: Diagrammatic and Graphical Presentation of Data
objectives: Select appropriate line, bar, pie and histogram displays.
Construct frequency polygon, curve and ogive.
Differentiate bar diagram and histogram.
Identify misleading graphical practices.
intro: A good graph communicates a pattern more quickly than a dense table. However, graphs can mislead when scales are truncated, areas are distorted or inappropriate chart types are chosen. Statistical graphics must therefore be accurate, labelled and suited to the variable type.
definition: Diagrammatic presentation uses visual forms such as bars and sectors, while graphical presentation uses coordinate axes to show distributions, trends or relationships.
need: To communicate patterns clearly.
To compare categories.
To show change over time.
To inspect distribution shape, skewness and outliers.

classification.name: Line diagram
classification.text: Values plotted against an ordered variable, commonly time, and connected by lines.

classification.name: Bar diagram
classification.text: Separated bars for discrete categories.

classification.name: Pie diagram
classification.text: A circle divided into sectors representing parts of a whole.

classification.name: Histogram
classification.text: Adjacent rectangles representing continuous class intervals.

classification.name: Frequency polygon
classification.text: Line joining class-midpoint frequencies.

classification.name: Ogive
classification.text: Cumulative-frequency curve.

explanation: Simple bar diagrams compare one series. Multiple bars compare two or more series. Component bars divide each total into parts; percentage bars standardise every total to 100.
In a pie diagram, each angle equals category value divided by total and multiplied by 360°. It is unsuitable when there are many categories or when values are close.
In a histogram, area represents frequency. For equal widths, height may be frequency. For unequal widths, height must be frequency density = frequency/class width.

A frequency polygon can be drawn through histogram midpoints or directly from midpoint-frequency pairs. A frequency curve is a smoothed polygon. Less-than and more-than ogives can be used to estimate median and quartiles.
Axes must show variables, units and sensible scales. Three-dimensional decoration should be avoided because perspective distorts magnitude.

Zoology: Bar diagram of species counts; histogram of fish lengths; line diagram of seasonal abundance.
Botany: Line graph of plant growth over time.
Microbiology: Bar diagram of antibiotic sensitivity.
Fisheries: Monthly catch line chart and species pie chart.

limitations: Exact values may be less visible than in tables.
Poor scales or decorative effects can mislead.
Pie charts are difficult to compare precisely.
precautions: Use accurate scales.
Start quantitative axes at zero for bars unless a break is clearly justified.
Label axes and units.
Use frequency density for unequal histogram widths.
Use patterns or labels in addition to colour.

examples.q: Values 20, 30 and 50 are shown in a pie chart. Find angles.
A class 0–10 has frequency 20 and class 10–30 has frequency 30. Find densities.
examples.answer: Histogram heights should be 2 and 1.5, not 20 and 30.

examples.q: Differentiate bar diagram and histogram.
steps: Bar gaps present; histogram bars touch.
Bar width arbitrary but equal; histogram area has statistical meaning.
Bar order may be rearranged; histogram order is numerical.
examples.answer: The displays serve different data structures.

misconceptions: Histogram and bar diagram are interchangeable.
The tallest bar in unequal-width histograms always has the highest frequency.
A graph without units is complete.
exam: Draw neat labelled diagrams.
Write construction steps and uses.
Include merits and limitations.
mnemonic: T-A-S-L: Title, Axes, Scale, Labels.
summary: Chart type must match data type and purpose.
Histogram area represents frequency.
Good graphics are accurate, simple and labelled.

formulae.name: Pie-sector angle
formulae.meaning: Converts a proportion into a circular sector.
formulae.use: Displaying a small number of parts of one whole.
formulae.avoid: Many categories or close values.
formulae.bio: Composition of fish species in a catch.

formulae.name: Frequency density
formulae.meaning: Frequency per unit width.
formulae.use: Histogram with unequal class widths.
formulae.avoid: Do not use raw frequency as height when widths differ.
formulae.bio: Length-frequency histogram with unequal size classes.

selfcheck: When is a line diagram preferred?
List four features of a good graph.
references: Tufte, E. R. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information. Graphics Press, Cheshire.
Gupta, S. P. Statistical Methods. Sultan Chand & Sons, New Delhi.

title: Measures of Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode
objectives: Calculate mean, median and mode for grouped and ungrouped data.
Select an appropriate average.
Explain formulae and symbols.
Interpret averages in biological context.
intro: A measure of central tendency is a single value intended to represent the centre or typical position of a dataset. No average is universally best. The arithmetic mean uses every observation, the median is positional and resistant to extremes, and the mode identifies the most frequent value or category.
definition: Central tendency is the tendency of observations to cluster around a central or representative value. The principal measures are arithmetic mean, median and mode.
need: To summarise a dataset.
To compare groups.
To provide a basis for dispersion and inferential methods.
To communicate a typical biological value.

classification.name: Arithmetic mean
classification.text: Sum of values divided by their number.

classification.name: Median
classification.text: Middle ordered value or interpolated central position.

classification.name: Mode
classification.text: Most frequent value, category or modal-class estimate.

classification.name: Weighted mean
classification.text: Mean in which observations or group means receive specified weights.

explanation: For ungrouped data, x̄ = Σx/n. For a discrete or grouped distribution, x̄ = Σfx/Σf. In continuous grouped data, class midpoints stand in for unknown individual values, so the result is an estimate.
For ungrouped data, arrange values. If n is odd, median is the (n+1)/2th value; if even, average the n/2th and (n/2+1)th values. For grouped continuous data, Median = L + [(N/2 − c.f.)/f]h.
For raw data, mode is the value with greatest frequency. For a continuous distribution with one clear modal class and approximately equal contiguous widths, Mode = L + [(f1−f0)/(2f1−f0−f2)]h.
The empirical relation Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean is only an approximation for moderately skewed unimodal distributions.

Mean is preferred for approximately symmetric quantitative data without severe outliers. Median is preferred for skewed or open-ended data. Mode is useful for nominal categories and the most common item.

Zoology: Mean fish length, median parasite count, modal shell-size class.
Botany: Mean plant height and median germination time.

intro: Two-sample comparisons are common in biology: a researcher may compare separate treatment groups or measure the same organisms before and after an intervention. These designs are not interchangeable. Independent-samples procedures analyse two unrelated groups, whereas a paired t-test analyses the within-pair differences. Welch's test is preferred when equal population variances cannot be assumed.
definition: An independent-samples t-test compares the means of two unrelated groups. The pooled form assumes equal population variances; Welch's form does not. A paired t-test is a one-sample t-test applied to the differences within matched pairs or repeated measurements.
need: To compare two independent biological groups.
To analyse before–after or matched observations without discarding pairing.

classification.name: Pooled independent t-test
classification.text: Compares two independent means under an equal-variance assumption.

classification.name: Welch independent t-test
classification.text: Compares two independent means without assuming equal variances; generally safer when sample sizes or SDs differ.

classification.name: Paired t-test
classification.text: Tests whether the mean of the within-pair differences differs from zero.

explanation: Independence is determined by design, not by numerical appearance. Fish assigned to two separate ponds are independent groups; the same fish measured before and after feeding are paired observations.

For Welch's test, the standard error is sqrt(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2), and the degrees of freedom are estimated by the Welch–Satterthwaite equation. This avoids the equal-variance assumption required by the pooled test.

For a paired test, calculate each difference di, then its mean d̄ and SD sd. The test statistic is t = d̄/(sd/√n), with df = n−1. The normality assumption applies to the differences, not separately to the two raw measurements.
A complete result reports group means and SDs, mean difference, confidence interval, t value, degrees of freedom, exact p-value and a biological interpretation.

explanation: Correlation quantifies how two variables vary together. In positive correlation both increase together, as fish length and weight do; in negative correlation one rises as the other falls, as water temperature and dissolved oxygen do. The coefficient lies between −1 and +1: the sign gives the direction and the magnitude gives the strength.

Simple correlation involves two variables, multiple correlation relates one variable to several together, and partial correlation measures the association between two variables while a third is held constant. The association may be linear or non-linear; only simple linear correlation is calculated in this course.

Always inspect the scatter plot before relying on a coefficient, because outliers and subgroups can strongly alter r. Correlation is symmetric (r for x with y equals r for y with x), whereas regression distinguishes predictor and response. A correlation does not establish causation: a third factor, such as season, may drive both variables.

explanation: A scatter diagram plots each pair of observations (x, y) as a point, with the explanatory variable conventionally on the x-axis. It reveals the form (linear or curved), direction, strength (how tightly the points cluster), groups and outliers.

In a linear relationship the points scatter about a straight line of constant slope. In a non-linear relationship they follow a curve, such as growth that levels off or a sigmoid dose–response. Pearson's r measures only linear association, so a strong curved relationship can give r close to zero. A transformation, such as logarithms for the length–weight relation W = aLᵇ, can sometimes linearise the pattern.

Check for subgroups (for example, pooled males and females can create a spurious trend), for outliers, and for spread that widens along the axis. Calculate and report r only after the plot has shown that a linear summary is reasonable.

Zoology: Plotting fish length against weight, on raw and logarithmic scales, before computing r.
Microbiology: Counts and response measurements.

Can be distorted by outliers

Avoid extrapolation

examples.q: Points rise from lower left to upper right in a narrow band. Describe the relationship.
examples.answer: Strong positive linear relationship.

examples.q: Growth rate rises with temperature, then falls (inverted U). Is Pearson's r appropriate?
examples.answer: No. The relationship is curved, so r may be near zero; use a curved model or a transformation.

examples.q: One point far from the rest reduces r from 0.9 to 0.5. What should be done?
examples.answer: Verify the point; do not delete it merely because it lowers r. Report the analysis both ways if it is genuine.

A curved pattern with r≈0 means the variables are unrelated.
Outliers may be deleted whenever they weaken the correlation.

title: Karl Pearson's Correlation Coefficient
objectives: Explain karl pearson's correlation coefficient clearly.
Apply the concept to biological data.
Interpret results without overstatement.
Answer university examination questions accurately.
intro: Pearson's r measures linear association from −1 to +1. It does not by itself establish causation.
definition: Pearson's r measures linear association from −1 to +1.
need: To describe relationships
To support interpretation and prediction
To prevent causal overstatement

classification.name: Positive
classification.text: Both variables tend to increase together.

classification.name: Negative
classification.text: One tends to decrease as the other increases.

classification.name: Zero/weak
classification.text: Little linear association.

classification.name: Linear/non-linear
classification.text: Straight-line versus curved pattern.

explanation: Pearson's r is Sxy/√(Sxx·Syy), where Sxy = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ), Sxx = Σ(x−x̄)² and Syy = Σ(y−ȳ)²; equivalently, r is the covariance divided by the product of the two SDs. It is unit-free and lies between −1 and +1, and it is unchanged when either variable is rescaled or shifted (for example from cm to mm).
Worked example: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. Here x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 4; the products (x−x̄)(y−ȳ) are 4, 0, 0, 0 and 2, so Sxy = 6; Sxx = 10 and Syy = 6. Therefore r = 6/√60 ≈ 0.775.

The square of r, the coefficient of determination, is the proportion of variation in y that is linearly accounted for by x; here r² = 0.60, or 60%. The method requires paired, independent, quantitative observations, an approximately linear pattern and no dominating outliers.

Zoology: Correlating body length with gill surface area across individuals of one fish species.
Microbiology: Counts and response measurements.

Can be distorted by outliers
precautions: Inspect scatter plot

If r = 0.6, what is r² and what does it mean?
examples.answer: r² = 0.36: 36% of the variation in y is linearly accounted for by x.

examples.q: Does r change when length is converted from cm to mm?
examples.answer: No. r is unit-free and unchanged by rescaling.

misconceptions: r = 0.8 means that 80% of the variation is explained (it is r² = 0.64).
r carries the units of the variables.
Pearson's r is suitable for any monotonic curve.

title: Interpretation, Significance and Limitations of Correlation
objectives: Explain interpretation, significance and limitations of correlation clearly.
Apply the concept to biological data.
Interpret results without overstatement.
Answer university examination questions accurately.
intro: Correlation must be interpreted with context, sample size, scatter pattern and possible confounding. It does not by itself establish causation.
definition: Correlation must be interpreted with context, sample size, scatter pattern and possible confounding.
need: To describe relationships
To support interpretation and prediction
To prevent causal overstatement

classification.name: Zero/weak

explanation: A rough guide to interpretation is that |r| below 0.3 is weak, 0.3 to 0.7 is moderate and above 0.7 is strong, but acceptable values depend on the field: biological measurements are usually noisier than physical ones, so the judgement must be made in context.

To test H₀: ρ = 0, use t = r√(n−2)/√(1−r²) with df = n−2. For r = 0.5 and n = 27, t = 0.5×5/0.866 ≈ 2.89 with df = 25, which exceeds the critical value 2.06, so p < 0.01. Significance depends on n: with very large samples a trivial r becomes significant, so report r with a confidence interval and judge its biological importance.

Limitations: correlation is not causation, because a confounder (for example, season driving both fish abundance and temperature) may produce it. A restricted range of x lowers r. Pooling distinct groups, correlating group means rather than individuals, or correlating ratios that share a component can all create misleading values. Outliers and non-linear patterns also distort r.

Zoology: Testing whether the length–weight correlation in a sample of 30 fish differs from zero.
Microbiology: Counts and response measurements.

examples.q: r = 0.5 from n = 27 pairs. Test H₀: ρ = 0 at α = 0.05.
examples.answer: t ≈ 2.89 > 2.06, so the correlation is significant (p < 0.01).

examples.q: r = 0.8 from n = 5 pairs. Is it significant at 5%?
examples.answer: t ≈ 2.31 < 3.18, so it is not significant; a high r from few pairs can arise by chance.

examples.q: Two traits correlate (r = 0.7) across ponds, but both rise with water temperature. Interpret.
examples.answer: Temperature may be a confounder, so the correlation does not show that one trait causes the other; examine partial correlation or a controlled study.

title: Regression Analysis: Lines and Equations
objectives: Explain regression as prediction of one variable from another.
Derive and use Y-on-X and X-on-Y regression equations.
Calculate regression coefficients, slope, intercept and residuals.
Distinguish prediction from correlation and recognise extrapolation risk.
intro: Regression analysis describes how the expected value of a response variable changes with a predictor and provides an equation for prediction. Unlike correlation, regression is directional: predicting fish weight from length is a different problem from predicting length from weight. The fitted line is chosen to minimise squared residuals in the response direction.
definition: A regression line is a fitted mathematical relationship used to estimate the expected value of one variable from another. In simple linear regression, Y-on-X is written Ŷ = a + b_yxX, where b_yx is the slope and a is the intercept.
need: To quantify change in a response per unit change in a predictor.
To predict biological measurements within the observed range.
To examine residuals and model adequacy.
To distinguish directional prediction from symmetric association.

classification.name: Regression of Y on X
classification.text: Predicts Y from a specified X and minimises vertical squared residuals.

classification.name: Regression of X on Y
classification.text: Predicts X from a specified Y and minimises horizontal squared residuals.

classification.name: Simple linear regression
classification.text: Uses one predictor and assumes an approximately straight-line mean relationship.

classification.name: Non-linear or multiple regression
classification.text: Enrichment methods used when the relationship is curved or several predictors are required.

explanation: For Y on X, b_yx = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(x−x̄)² = r(sy/sx), and a = ȳ − b_yx x̄. The fitted equation passes through (x̄,ȳ).
For X on Y, b_xy = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)/Σ(y−ȳ)² = r(sx/sy), and the equation is X̂ = a' + b_xyY. The two regression lines are generally different and should not be interchanged.
A residual is e = y − ŷ. Residual plots help detect curvature, unequal spread and unusual observations. A fitted line is not automatically valid for extrapolation beyond the observed X range.
The regression coefficients have the same sign as r and satisfy b_xy b_yx = r². If |r|=1, the two regression lines coincide; if r=0, they are perpendicular at the means.

Zoology: Predict animal mass from body length.
Biotechnology: Construct a calibration equation for concentration from absorbance.
Microbiology: Predict colony density from optical density within the calibrated range.
Medicine: Estimate a response from a continuous predictor while noting uncertainty.
Agriculture: Predict yield from rainfall within observed conditions.
Environmental science: Predict pollutant concentration from an instrument signal.

advantages: Quantifies the expected response change per predictor unit.
limitations: Prediction may be poor outside the observed range.
Outliers and influential points can alter slope.
Association alone does not establish causation.
Linear regression may be inappropriate for curved or heteroscedastic data.
precautions: Specify response and predictor before fitting.
Inspect the scatter and residual plots.
Retain units in the slope interpretation.
Avoid extrapolation.
Report equation, r or R², sample size and uncertainty.

examples.q: Interpret Ŷ = 5 + 2X when X is fish length in cm and Y is weight in g.
steps: Slope 2 means predicted weight increases by 2 g per additional cm.
Intercept 5 g is the predicted value at X=0, which may lie outside the data range.
examples.answer: Use the slope biologically; do not overinterpret an unrealistic intercept.

examples.q: Given x̄=10, ȳ=25 and b_yx=1.8, find the Y-on-X equation.
examples.answer: The fitted Y-on-X equation is Ŷ = 7 + 1.8X.

examples.q: For X: 1,2,3,4 and Y: 2,3,5,6, calculate the Y-on-X line.
examples.answer: The regression line is Ŷ = 0.5 + 1.4X; prediction at X=5 is 7.5, provided X=5 is not an unsafe extrapolation.

misconceptions: Regression and correlation are interchangeable.
The Y-on-X equation can always be reversed algebraically to predict X.
A high R² proves causation.
A prediction outside the observed range is equally reliable.
exam: Define response, predictor, slope, intercept and residual.
Write both regression equations and coefficient formulae.
Show that the lines pass through (x̄,ȳ).
Include a worked biological prediction and limitation of extrapolation.
mnemonic: Choose the response first; regress the response on the predictor.
summary: Regression is directional and predictive.
Y-on-X and X-on-Y are different equations.
Slope has units and gives expected response change.
Residuals and the observed range determine model usefulness.

title: Introduction to Computers, Applications and Types
objectives: Define a computer and distinguish data from information.
Classify computers by data handling (analog, digital, hybrid), size and purpose.
Distinguish hardware from software and name the input–process–output–storage cycle.
Give biological examples where each class of computer is used.
intro: A computer is an electronic programmable system that accepts input, processes data, stores information and produces output. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: Charles Babbage designed the programmable Analytical Engine in the 1830s, though it was never completed. Electronic general-purpose computers such as ENIAC (1945–46) followed, and microprocessor-based personal computers became common from the late 1970s.
definition: A computer is an electronic programmable system that accepts input, processes data, stores information and produces output.
need: To understand what a computer can and cannot do before using it for research data.
To choose suitable equipment (laptop, server, embedded controller) for a laboratory or field task.
To separate a computer's speed and accuracy from the correctness of the data entered into it.

classification.name: Analog computer
classification.text: Processes continuously varying physical quantities.

classification.name: Digital computer
classification.text: Processes discrete binary data and instructions.

classification.name: Hybrid computer
classification.text: Combines analog measurement with digital control.

classification.name: Microcomputer and embedded system
classification.text: General-purpose personal device or dedicated controller within equipment.

explanation: A computer accepts data through input devices, processes instructions, stores data and produces information through output devices. Hardware comprises physical components; software comprises instructions and data.

Computers are classified by data handling, size, purpose and performance. Supercomputers support large scientific calculations, mainframes serve many users and transactions, personal computers support individual work, and embedded computers control devices.

Zoology: Storing specimen records, analysing growth or behaviour data and preparing reports.
Botany: Image analysis of leaf area and herbarium databases.
Microbiology: Colony counting software and growth-curve fitting.
Medicine: Hospital information systems and imaging devices.
Agriculture: Weather-station data loggers and farm-management records.
Environmental science: Remote sensors, GIS mapping and climate modelling.

advantages: High speed and consistent accuracy for repetitive calculation.
Large, searchable storage of observations and literature.
Automation of data capture through connected instruments.
limitations: A computer processes only the data and instructions it is given (garbage in, garbage out).
It has no biological judgement; interpretation remains the scientist's task.
Hardware failure, power loss and software faults can destroy work.
precautions: Keep tested backups of raw data.
Record the software name and version used for an analysis.
Check results against a simple hand calculation.
Use surge protection or an uninterruptible power supply for important work.

examples.q: Distinguish data from information using a biological example.
steps: Data: raw values such as 12.1, 11.8, 13.0 g (body masses).
Information: the processed result, 'mean body mass = 12.3 g'.
examples.answer: Data are unprocessed facts; information is data processed into a meaningful form.

examples.q: A data logger in a pond records temperature every 10 minutes. How many readings are stored in 24 hours?
examples.answer: 144 readings (145 if both the first and last instants of the day are recorded).

examples.q: Classify (i) a pocket calculator, (ii) an ICU patient monitor that converts a continuous pressure signal to numbers, (iii) the controller inside an incubator.
steps: (ii) Hybrid: analog sensing with digital processing.
(iii) Embedded system: dedicated to one task.
examples.answer: (i) digital, (ii) hybrid, (iii) embedded.

Every electronic device is a general-purpose computer.
Hardware alone can perform useful work without software.
exam: Define computer and list its four basic functions.
Draw the input–process–output–storage block diagram.
Classify computers with one example of each.
Give two biological applications.
mnemonic: IPOS: Input, Process, Output, Storage.
summary: A computer is an electronic programmable system that accepts input, processes data, stores information and produces output.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.

V. Rajaraman, Fundamentals of Computers. PHI Learning, New Delhi.

title: Generations of Computers
objectives: Name the key technology of each computer generation.
Explain why successive technologies made computers smaller, faster and more reliable.
State that generation dates are approximate and overlapping.
Relate generations to the spread of computing in laboratories.
intro: Computer generations classify major stages of hardware technology from vacuum tubes to microprocessors and intelligent systems. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: ENIAC (1945) used about 17,000 vacuum tubes. The transistor was invented at Bell Laboratories in 1947, the integrated circuit was demonstrated in 1958–59, and Intel's 4004 (1971) was the first commercial microprocessor.
definition: Computer generations classify major stages of hardware technology from vacuum tubes to microprocessors and intelligent systems.
need: To understand why modern devices differ so greatly from early machines.
To answer examination questions that ask for characteristics of each generation.
To see computing as a continuing technological development rather than a fixed set of devices.

classification.name: First generation
classification.text: Vacuum tubes; large size, high heat and machine language.

classification.name: Second generation
classification.text: Transistors; smaller, more reliable and less power-consuming.

classification.name: Third generation
classification.text: Integrated circuits and improved operating systems.

classification.name: Fourth generation
classification.text: Microprocessors, personal computers and networks.

classification.name: Fifth-generation direction
classification.text: Parallel processing, AI-oriented systems and advanced interfaces.

explanation: A generation denotes a major change in the dominant electronic technology, not a rigid boundary that makes older machines disappear immediately.
Progress involved smaller components, greater reliability, lower cost, higher speed, larger memory and more accessible programming environments.

Zoology: Early mainframes processed census-type tables; today laptops handle field data.
Botany: Plant-survey databases moved from card files to spreadsheets.
Biotechnology: Sequencing became feasible only with high-speed fourth-generation hardware.
Microbiology: Automated colony counters rely on microprocessors.
Medicine: Computed tomography needs fast processing from the third generation onward.
Agriculture: Farm sensors depend on low-power microprocessors.
Fisheries: Echo-sounders and fish-finders use embedded chips.
Environmental science: Satellite data processing uses parallel high-performance systems.

advantages: Each generation reduced size, power use and cost per calculation.
Reliability improved when moving parts and fragile tubes were replaced.
Programming became easier through high-level languages and operating systems.
limitations: Generation labels are conventional and overlap in time.
The fifth generation is a research direction, not a single hardware change.
Newer technology does not remove the need for correct programs and data.
precautions: Memorise the technology, not exact dates alone.
Do not state that each generation began on one fixed year.
Link each generation to a feature (size, speed, memory).

examples.q: Arrange in order: integrated circuit, vacuum tube, microprocessor, transistor.
examples.answer: Vacuum tube → transistor → integrated circuit → microprocessor.

examples.q: Why did transistors improve on vacuum tubes?
steps: Transistors need no heated filament, so they use less power and give off less heat.
They are smaller and fail less often.
examples.answer: Smaller size, lower power, less heat and greater reliability.

examples.q: A student states 'the fourth generation began in 1971 everywhere'. Critique this.
steps: Adoption was gradual and overlapped with third-generation machines.
examples.answer: Generation dates are approximate; the statement overstates precision.

misconceptions: Each generation began worldwide on one exact date.
Fifth generation means that all computers possess human intelligence.
Software development is unrelated to hardware generations.
exam: Tabulate the five generations with technology and features.
Explain why dates are approximate.
Give one advantage of each generation over the previous one.
mnemonic: Tubes, Transistors, ICs, Microprocessors, then AI: T-T-I-M-A.
summary: Computer generations classify major stages of hardware technology from vacuum tubes to microprocessors and intelligent systems.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.
selfcheck: Name the key technology of each generation.
references: P. K. Sinha and Priti Sinha, Computer Fundamentals. BPB Publications, New Delhi.
V. Rajaraman, Fundamentals of Computers. PHI Learning, New Delhi.

title: Input Devices
objectives: Classify input devices by the kind of data they capture.
Distinguish OCR, OMR and barcode/QR readers.
Calculate pixel count and uncompressed size of a scanned image.
Select an input device for a laboratory or field task.
intro: Input devices convert user actions or physical signals into data a computer can process. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: Hollerith's punched-card tabulator was used in the 1890 US census. The computer mouse was demonstrated by Douglas Engelbart in 1968, and touchscreens became mainstream on phones in the 2000s.
definition: Input devices convert user actions or physical signals into data a computer can process.
need: To get observations into a computer accurately and efficiently.
To choose a device that suits data type, volume and environment.
To recognise sources of error such as poor calibration or low resolution.

classification.name: Text and pointing input
classification.text: Keyboard, mouse, touchpad and touchscreen.

classification.name: Image and code capture
classification.text: Scanner, camera, OCR, OMR and barcode/QR readers.

classification.name: Audio and biometric input
classification.text: Microphone, fingerprint and other sensors.

classification.name: Scientific input
classification.text: Data loggers, probes, GPS and laboratory instruments.

explanation: Input devices translate human actions or physical signals into machine-readable data. Selection depends on data type, speed, accuracy, environment and accessibility.
OCR recognises printed characters, OMR detects marked positions, and barcode readers decode patterned identifiers; these technologies are not interchangeable.

Zoology: Camera-trap images, field GPS loggers and audio recorders for bird calls.
Microbiology: Digital microscope cameras for colony images.
Medicine: Biometric ID and barcode wristbands for patients.
Agriculture: Soil-moisture and weather sensors feeding a logger.
Fisheries: Barcode tags on sample vials and fish tags.
Environmental science: Water-quality probes, GPS and drone cameras.

advantages: Speeds up data entry and reduces transcription errors.
Captures data directly from instruments and the field.
Supports accessibility through voice and touch input.
limitations: Accuracy depends on calibration, resolution and the environment.
OCR output may misread characters and needs checking.
Sensors drift over time and need maintenance.
precautions: Calibrate probes and sensors before use.
Scan at a resolution suited to the purpose.
Proof-read OCR output against the original.
Label files with date, site and sample code immediately.

examples.q: Classify keyboard, scanner, microphone, GPS receiver.
examples.answer: All are input devices, each capturing a different data type.

examples.q: A 4 × 6 inch photograph is scanned at 600 dpi. Calculate the pixel dimensions and the pixel count.
examples.answer: 2400 × 3600 pixels ≈ 8.64 megapixels.

examples.q: Estimate the uncompressed size of that 24-bit colour scan.
examples.answer: ≈ 25.9 MB (decimal), which is why scans are normally compressed.

misconceptions: OCR and OMR perform the same task.
A touchscreen is only an output device.
Higher resolution automatically guarantees accurate scientific measurement.
exam: Classify input devices with examples.
Differentiate OCR, OMR and MICR.
Explain two biological uses of sensors as input devices.
mnemonic: OCR reads characters; OMR reads marks.
summary: Input devices convert user actions or physical signals into data a computer can process.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.

title: Output Devices
objectives: Distinguish soft-copy from hard-copy output.
Compare impact, laser and inkjet printers.
Explain screen resolution, size and refresh rate.
Calculate pixel counts for screens and print sizes.
intro: Output devices present processed information in visual, printed, audio or other usable form. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: Laser printing was developed at Xerox in the early 1970s, and inkjet printers became widely available to consumers in the 1980s.
definition: Output devices present processed information in visual, printed, audio or other usable form.
need: To present results in a usable visual, printed or audible form.
To choose a printer or display for a specific purpose and budget.
To avoid confusing physical size with resolution.

classification.name: Soft-copy visual output
classification.text: Monitor, projector and display panel.

classification.name: Hard-copy output
classification.text: Printers and plotters.

classification.name: Audio and tactile output
classification.text: Speakers, headphones and haptic devices.

explanation: Output devices convert processed data into a form usable by people or other systems. Monitor quality is described by resolution, colour depth, refresh rate and size.
Impact printers strike a ribbon; non-impact printers such as laser and inkjet operate without mechanical impact. Plotters are suited to large technical drawings.

Zoology: Printing posters and projecting specimen images in seminars.
Botany: Large plotter drawings of plant distribution maps.
Biotechnology: Printing gel images and displaying sequence alignments.
Microbiology: Viewing stained slide images on high-resolution displays.
Medicine: Printing prescriptions and displaying scan images.
Fisheries: Plotting survey maps and charts of catch data.

advantages: Allows results to be shared, filed and presented.
Hard copy is independent of power and software.
Audio and tactile output improves accessibility.
limitations: Colour on screen and on paper may differ.
Inkjet cartridges and toner add running cost.
Low-resolution output hides fine detail.
precautions: Use print preview before printing.
Set the correct paper size and orientation.
Match the output format to the audience (screen vs print).
Use recycled paper and double-sided printing where suitable.

examples.q: Classify monitor, projector, laser printer, speaker.

All printers produce the same permanence and quality.
A projector stores the presentation being shown.

title: CPU, ALU, Control Unit, Registers and Motherboard
objectives: Describe the functions of the ALU, control unit and registers.
State the fetch–decode–execute–store cycle.
Name the data, address and control buses.
Interpret clock rate and address width in simple calculations.
intro: The CPU executes instructions; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic; the control unit coordinates operations; registers hold immediate data. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: John von Neumann's 1945 report on the EDVAC described the stored-program design still used today. Placing a whole CPU on one chip began with the Intel 4004 in 1971.
definition: The CPU executes instructions; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic; the control unit coordinates operations; registers hold immediate data.
need: To understand how instructions are executed inside a computer.
To interpret processor specifications when selecting equipment.
To understand why speed depends on more than clock rate.

classification.name: ALU
classification.text: Performs arithmetic, comparison and logical operations.

classification.name: Control unit
classification.text: Fetches and decodes instructions and coordinates data movement.

classification.name: Registers
classification.text: Very fast small storage inside the CPU.

classification.name: Motherboard and buses
classification.text: Connect CPU, memory, storage and expansion devices through data, address and control paths.

explanation: The instruction cycle consists broadly of fetch, decode, execute and store. The program counter identifies the next instruction, while the instruction register holds the current instruction.
Clock rate alone does not determine performance; architecture, cores, cache, memory speed and software workload also matter.

Zoology: Running population-viability simulations.
Botany: Image processing of leaf and root scans.
Biotechnology: Genome assembly needs many cores and large memory.
Microbiology: Fast fitting of growth curves.

advantages: Cache reduces waiting for slower memory.
limitations: Heat and power limit clock speed.
A fast CPU is held back by slow memory or storage.
Software must be written to use multiple cores.
precautions: Compare processors by cores, cache and workload, not clock rate alone.
Keep the cooling system clean.
Do not state that the CPU is the whole cabinet.

examples.q: List the stages of the instruction cycle.
steps: Decode it in the control unit.
examples.answer: Fetch → decode → execute → store.

examples.q: A 3.0 GHz processor averages 2 clock cycles per instruction. How many instructions per second?
examples.answer: 1.5 billion instructions per second.

examples.q: A 32-bit address bus can address how many bytes of memory?
examples.answer: 4 GiB of byte-addressable memory.

misconceptions: The CPU is the entire computer cabinet.
A higher clock speed always means a faster computer.
RAM is located inside the CPU registers.
exam: Draw the block diagram of a CPU.
Explain the functions of ALU and control unit.
Differentiate data, address and control buses.
mnemonic: ALU computes, CU controls, registers remember.
summary: The CPU executes instructions; the ALU performs arithmetic and logic; the control unit coordinates operations; registers hold immediate data.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.

title: Primary Memory, Secondary Memory and Storage Devices
objectives: Distinguish RAM, ROM, cache and secondary storage.
Explain volatile and non-volatile memory.
Compare HDD, SSD and optical media.
Convert storage units and plan backups.
intro: Primary memory is directly accessible to the CPU, while secondary storage retains data for long-term use. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: Magnetic core memory dominated in the 1950s and the IBM RAMAC (1956) was an early hard-disk system. Flash memory was invented at Toshiba in the 1980s and now underlies SSDs and pen drives.
definition: Primary memory is directly accessible to the CPU, while secondary storage retains data for long-term use.
need: To store data safely and retrieve it quickly.
To choose an appropriate balance of speed, capacity and cost.
To prevent loss of research data.

classification.name: RAM
classification.text: Volatile read/write working memory used by active programs.

classification.name: ROM and firmware
classification.text: Non-volatile memory holding startup or device instructions.

classification.name: Cache
classification.text: Small high-speed memory close to the CPU.

classification.name: Secondary storage
classification.text: HDD, SSD, optical and removable media for long-term retention.

explanation: Memory hierarchy balances speed, capacity and cost: registers and cache are fastest and smallest; RAM is larger but volatile; secondary storage is slower and persistent.
An SSD has no moving parts and generally offers faster access and better shock resistance than an HDD, but backup remains necessary because any device can fail.

Zoology: Storing field photographs and call recordings.
Biotechnology: Storing sequence reads of many gigabytes.
Microbiology: Storing microscope image stacks.
Medicine: Storing patient records with access control.
Agriculture: Storing farm records on cloud and local drives.
Fisheries: Archiving catch records and tagging data.
Environmental science: Storing satellite imagery and time series.

advantages: Cloud storage allows sharing and remote access.
Hierarchical memory gives speed and capacity together.
limitations: RAM loses content without power.
Every device can fail, including SSDs.
Cloud storage depends on connectivity and privacy terms.
precautions: Follow the 3-2-1 backup rule: three copies, two media types, one off-site.
Test restores regularly.
Eject removable media safely.
Encrypt drives that hold sensitive data.

examples.q: Which is volatile: RAM or ROM?
steps: RAM loses its content when power is removed.
examples.answer: RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile.

examples.q: A field team saves 500 photographs of 4 MB each. What total storage is needed?
examples.answer: About 2 GB.

examples.q: A drive sold as 1 TB shows about 931 GB in the operating system. Explain.
steps: The operating system divides by 2³⁰: 10¹²/2³⁰ ≈ 931 GiB.
examples.answer: Decimal vs binary units; no storage is missing.

misconceptions: More storage capacity always makes processing faster.
RAM permanently stores files after power-off.
Cloud storage removes the need for local backup and security.
exam: Differentiate primary and secondary memory.
Explain the memory hierarchy.
Compare HDD and SSD.
Describe the 3-2-1 backup rule.
mnemonic: RAM remembers only while powered.
summary: Primary memory is directly accessible to the CPU, while secondary storage retains data for long-term use.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.

title: Operating Systems: Windows, Linux, Unix and Android
objectives: List the main functions of an operating system.
Compare Windows, Linux, Unix and Android.
Explain files, directories and permissions.
Interpret a Linux permission code such as 754.
intro: An operating system manages hardware, files, processes, memory, security and user interaction. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: Unix was developed at Bell Laboratories from 1969 by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie. Windows 1.0 appeared in 1985, the Linux kernel was released by Linus Torvalds in 1991, and the first Android phone reached the market in 2008.
definition: An operating system manages hardware, files, processes, memory, security and user interaction.
need: To understand how applications use hardware through the operating system.
To select a suitable system for desktop, server or mobile work.
To protect files through accounts and permissions.

classification.name: Windows
classification.text: Commercial desktop operating-system family with graphical administration tools.

classification.name: GNU/Linux
classification.text: Open-source Unix-like systems distributed in many variants.

classification.name: Unix
classification.text: Multiuser, multitasking operating-system family influential in servers and research.

classification.name: Android
classification.text: Linux-kernel-based mobile operating system with an application framework.

explanation: An operating system manages processes, memory, files, devices, users, permissions and the user interface. It provides services between applications and hardware.
A file system organises data into files and directories. User accounts and permissions restrict access; updates correct defects and security vulnerabilities.

Zoology: Linux servers for bioinformatics pipelines.
Botany: Windows or Linux desktops running image-analysis software.
Biotechnology: Linux clusters for phylogenetics and genomics.
Microbiology: Instrument computers running Windows control software.
Medicine: Hospital systems with controlled user accounts.
Agriculture: Android phones for field-data collection apps.
Environmental science: Linux servers for model runs and data portals.

advantages: Multitasking and memory management let many programs run safely.
Open-source systems are inspectable and adaptable.
limitations: Software compatibility differs between systems.
Unpatched systems are vulnerable to attack.
Mobile apps run in sandboxes with limited file access.
precautions: Install updates promptly.
Use a standard user account for daily work.
Review app permissions on Android.
Do not run unknown programs with administrator rights.

examples.q: Name four functions of an operating system.
examples.answer: The OS manages processes, memory, files, devices and security.

examples.q: Interpret the Linux permission code 754.
examples.answer: Owner can read, write and execute; group can read and execute; others can only read.

examples.q: Why is Android described as Linux-based but not identical to desktop Linux?
steps: Android uses a modified Linux kernel.
Its application framework, libraries and security model differ.
examples.answer: They share a kernel family but not the full user-space system.

misconceptions: An operating system is the same as an application program.
Linux has only a command-line interface.
Android applications have unrestricted access to all files.
exam: Define an operating system and list its functions.
Compare Windows and Linux.
Explain file permissions.
mnemonic: OS = Manager between hardware and applications.
summary: An operating system manages hardware, files, processes, memory, security and user interaction.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.
selfcheck: Compare Windows, Linux, Unix and Android.
