Distinguish lossless and lossy compression.
Calculate the uncompressed size of audio and video.
Apply copyright and accessibility practice.
intro: Multimedia integrates text, graphics, audio, video, animation and interactivity. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: The compact disc (1982) introduced mass-market digital audio. JPEG (1992) and MP3 (standardised in 1993 as MPEG-1 Layer III) made efficient lossy compression common.
definition: Multimedia integrates text, graphics, audio, video, animation and interactivity.
need: To prepare effective teaching and presentation material.
To balance quality against file size.
To produce accessible, lawful educational media.

classification.name: Text and graphics
classification.text: Written content, diagrams, photographs and illustrations.

classification.name: Audio and video
classification.text: Recorded sound and moving images.

classification.name: Animation and interactivity
classification.text: Simulated motion and user-controlled response.

classification.name: Compression
classification.text: Lossless or lossy reduction of file size.

explanation: Multimedia combines several media types to communicate information. Resolution, frame rate, sampling rate, bit depth and compression affect quality and file size.

Lossless compression preserves all information; lossy compression discards selected information for greater size reduction. Copyright, captioning and alternative text are essential in educational media.

Zoology: Video of animal behaviour and recorded bird calls.
Microbiology: Time-lapse microscopy of cell division.
Environmental science: Photo and video documentation for conservation.

advantages: Combining text, images and sound can aid understanding.
Compression makes storage and sharing practical.
limitations: Large files strain storage and bandwidth.
Lossy compression cannot be reversed.
Poor design can distract rather than help.
precautions: Use only media you are licensed to use and cite sources.
Add captions and alternative text.
Keep an uncompressed master of important images.
Avoid excessive animation.

examples.q: Classify a photograph, a lecture recording, a narration clip.
examples.answer: Graphic, video and audio respectively.

examples.q: Compute the data rate of uncompressed CD audio (44,100 Hz, 16 bit, 2 channels).
examples.answer: ≈ 1.41 Mbit/s, about 10.6 MB per minute.

examples.q: Estimate the raw data rate of 1920 × 1080, 24-bit, 30 frames/s video and say why compression is needed.
examples.answer: ≈ 187 MB/s, far too large to store or stream without compression.

misconceptions: A larger file is always higher quality.
Compression always destroys visible quality.
Adding animation automatically improves learning.

Differentiate lossless and lossy compression.
Explain copyright and accessibility in educational media.

summary: Multimedia integrates text, graphics, audio, video, animation and interactivity.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.

title: Artificial Intelligence: Concepts, Uses and Limitations
objectives: Define AI, machine learning and generative AI.
Calculate sensitivity, specificity and accuracy for a classifier.
Explain bias, overfitting and the need for verification.
Identify suitable and unsuitable uses of AI in life sciences.
intro: Artificial intelligence comprises computational methods that perform tasks involving learning, prediction, recognition, language or decision support. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop. Deep-learning image recognition advanced sharply after 2012, and generative AI tools became widely available in the 2020s.
definition: Artificial intelligence comprises computational methods that perform tasks involving learning, prediction, recognition, language or decision support.
need: To use AI tools in research responsibly.
To judge claims about AI performance critically.
To recognise limitations such as bias and fabricated output.

classification.name: Machine learning
classification.text: Algorithms learn patterns from data for prediction or classification.

classification.name: Computer vision
classification.text: Methods analyse images and video.

classification.name: Natural-language processing
classification.text: Methods analyse or generate human language.

classification.name: Generative AI
classification.text: Models create new text, images, audio or other content from learned patterns.

explanation: AI systems depend on training data, objectives and evaluation. Their outputs are probabilistic and may contain bias, fabricated details or errors.

In life sciences AI can classify species images, assist microscopy, analyse sequences and support decision-making, but human verification, privacy protection and transparent reporting remain necessary.

Zoology: Identifying species from camera-trap images.
Botany: Recognising plant diseases from leaf photographs.
Biotechnology: Predicting protein structure and variant effects.
Microbiology: Classifying bacterial colonies in images.
Agriculture: Crop yield prediction from satellite data.
Environmental science: Detecting land-cover change and acoustic monitoring.

advantages: Processes large image and sequence collections quickly.
Can reveal patterns not obvious to the eye.
limitations: Training-data bias produces biased results.
Generative models can state fabricated facts or references.
Performance often drops on new data (overfitting).
precautions: Verify AI output against primary sources.
Never upload confidential or personal data to public tools.
Report which tool and version you used.
Test on data not used for training.

steps: A computer learns patterns from example data.

examples.answer: Machine learning builds models from data rather than hand-written rules.

misconceptions: AI output is automatically factual.
A high training accuracy guarantees real-world performance.
AI removes the need for subject expertise and ethical responsibility.

title: Cybersecurity, Privacy and Safe Computing
objectives: Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Recognise phishing, malware and ransomware.
Apply strong passwords, MFA, updates and backups.
Compute the size of a password search space.
intro: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, disruption, alteration or loss. Computers support biological data analysis, documentation, communication and instrumentation.
history: The Morris worm of 1988 was one of the first major internet worms and led to organised incident response. Phishing and ransomware have since grown into widespread threats.
definition: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, disruption, alteration or loss.
need: To protect research data and personal accounts.
To recognise and avoid common attacks.
To use computers legally and ethically.

classification.name: Threats
classification.text: Malware, phishing, social engineering, ransomware and unauthorised access.

classification.name: Controls
classification.text: Strong authentication, updates, backups, encryption and least privilege.

classification.name: Privacy
classification.text: Responsible collection, use, storage and sharing of personal data.

classification.name: Incident response
classification.text: Detection, containment, recovery and reporting after a security event.

explanation: Cybersecurity protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. A strong unique password plus multifactor authentication reduces account compromise.
Phishing messages imitate trusted sources to steal credentials or deliver malware. Backups should be tested and at least one copy should be isolated from routine access.

Zoology: Protecting unpublished field data and animal-ethics records.
Microbiology: Securing lab instrument computers.
Agriculture: Protecting farm financial and cooperative records.

advantages: Prevents loss, theft and alteration of data.
Maintains trust of participants and collaborators.
limitations: No single tool gives complete protection.
Security can reduce convenience.
Human error remains the main weakness.
precautions: Use unique passwords with a password manager and MFA.
Check sender and link before clicking.
Keep tested offline backups.
Install updates and avoid pirated software.

examples.q: State the CIA triad.
examples.answer: Confidentiality, integrity and availability.

examples.q: Compare the search space of an 8-character password from 62 symbols with a 12-character password from 94 symbols.
examples.answer: The longer password has about two billion times more combinations.

examples.q: An email says 'Your account will close in 2 hours. Click here.' List warning signs.
examples.answer: These indicate phishing; go to the official site directly and report it.

misconceptions: Antivirus alone provides complete security.
A familiar logo proves an email is genuine.
Deleting a local file removes every copy from cloud or backup systems.
exam: Explain the CIA triad.
List cyber threats and preventive measures.
Describe safe password practice.
mnemonic: CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.
summary: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, disruption, alteration or loss.
Responsible use requires security, backup and verification.

history: Dedicated word-processing machines of the 1970s gave way to software on personal computers in the 1980s, and office suites then combined word processing, spreadsheets and presentations.
definition: Office automation uses computer applications to create, process, store, retrieve and communicate office information efficiently.
need: To keep project files organised and retrievable.
To avoid loss and confusion between versions.
To produce documents in formats others can open.

classification.name: Word processing

classification.name: Spreadsheet
classification.text: Tabular calculation, analysis and charting.

classification.name: Presentation software
classification.text: Slide-based visual communication.

classification.name: Communication and storage tools
classification.text: Email, browsers, cloud/local file systems and collaboration platforms.

explanation: Office automation integrates software, files, devices and procedures to reduce repetitive work and improve accuracy. A sound folder structure, meaningful filenames and version control prevent loss and confusion.
File extensions identify formats such as .docx, .xlsx, .pptx and .pdf. 'Save' updates the current file; 'Save As' creates a new name, format or location.

Zoology: Organising field-trip data, photographs and reports by date and site.
Biotechnology: Keeping protocols, raw data and results in a consistent tree.
Microbiology: Filing culture records and SOP versions.
Medicine: Maintaining patient-record files under confidentiality rules.
Agriculture: Organising trial data by season and plot.

Version names prevent overwriting good work.
Standard formats such as PDF give reliable sharing.
limitations: Naming rules work only if everyone follows them.

Cloud folders may sync mistakes as well as correct work.

Keep raw data separate and read-only.
Back up to a second device or cloud.

To edit without damaging structure.

title: Probability: Basic Concepts, Rules and the Normal Distribution
objectives: Define random experiment, sample space, event and the three approaches to probability.
Apply the addition and multiplication rules and conditional probability to biological examples.
Describe the normal distribution, its parameters and the empirical (68–95–99.7) rule.
Explain why the normal distribution underlies most parametric tests used elsewhere in this course.
intro: Every hypothesis test in this course rests on probability. A p-value is a probability, a level of significance is a probability threshold, and the t and chi-square distributions are themselves probability distributions. Before hypothesis testing can be used with confidence, the basic vocabulary and rules of probability, together with the normal distribution, must be understood clearly.
history: Classical probability theory developed from the study of games of chance by Pascal and Fermat in the seventeenth century. Carl Friedrich Gauss and Pierre-Simon Laplace later described the normal (Gaussian) distribution, which became central to statistical inference through the work of Fisher, Gosset and Pearson.
definition: Probability is a numerical measure, between 0 and 1, of how likely an event is to occur. The normal distribution is a continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution defined completely by its mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ).
need: To quantify uncertainty before it can be used in formal hypothesis testing.
To understand what a p-value and a significance level actually represent.
To justify why sample means from many biological measurements behave approximately normally.
To interpret risk, odds and diagnostic accuracy in later applied topics.

classification.name: Classical probability
classification.text: Based on equally likely outcomes: P(A) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes.

classification.name: Empirical (relative frequency) probability
classification.text: Based on observed long-run frequency of an event in repeated trials or field data.

classification.name: Subjective probability
classification.text: A reasoned degree of belief when repeated trials are not possible.

classification.name: Independent vs dependent events
classification.text: Independent events do not affect each other's occurrence; dependent events do.

explanation: A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment; an event is any subset of the sample space. Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so their probabilities simply add.

The addition rule for any two events is P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B); the subtraction removes the double-counted overlap. For independent events, the multiplication rule P(A∩B) = P(A)×P(B) applies, and conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) measures how the probability of A changes once B is known to have occurred.

The normal distribution is symmetric about μ; roughly 68% of values lie within one SD, 95% within two SD, and 99.7% within three SD of the mean (the empirical rule). Converting a value to a z-score, z = (x−μ)/σ, expresses it as the number of standard deviations from the mean, allowing comparison across different variables and scales.

Many biological measurements are approximately normal, and the Central Limit Theorem shows that the sampling distribution of a mean tends towards normality as sample size increases, even when the underlying data are not perfectly normal. This is the theoretical justification for using t-tests, ANOVA and confidence intervals elsewhere in this course.

Zoology: Estimating the probability that a randomly caught fish exceeds a minimum legal length.
Botany: Modelling the proportion of seeds expected to germinate under standard conditions.
Biotechnology: Assessing the probability of a rare mutation appearing in a screened colony.
Microbiology: Estimating the chance of contamination given historical plate-count frequencies.
Medicine: Interpreting diagnostic test sensitivity and specificity as conditional probabilities.
Agriculture: Predicting the probability of yield falling below a threshold given historical variability.
Fisheries: Modelling size-at-capture using a normal approximation for stock assessment.
Environmental science: Estimating the probability that a pollutant reading exceeds a safety limit.

advantages: Provides the formal basis for every later inferential method in this course.
The normal distribution allows probabilities to be read from a single standardised table.
limitations: Not every biological variable is normally distributed; skewed data need transformation or non-parametric methods.
Classical probability requires genuinely equally likely outcomes, which is rare outside idealised examples.
precautions: Distinguish independent from mutually exclusive events; they are not the same.
Check whether a variable is even approximately normal before relying on the empirical rule.
State whether a stated probability is classical, empirical or subjective.
Do not interpret a z-score as a percentage without consulting the standard normal table or software.

title: One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
objectives: Explain why comparing more than two group means requires ANOVA rather than repeated t-tests.
Partition total variation into between-groups and within-groups components.
Calculate the F statistic and interpret it against its reference distribution.
State the assumptions of one-way ANOVA and describe the role of post-hoc tests.
intro: When three or more independent groups must be compared, running a separate t-test for every pair inflates the overall chance of a false-positive result. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) tests all group means simultaneously with a single, appropriately controlled test.
history: One-way ANOVA was developed by Ronald A. Fisher in the 1920s for agricultural field-trial comparisons and remains one of the most widely used methods for comparing multiple experimental groups in biology.
definition: One-way ANOVA tests the null hypothesis that the means of two or more independent groups, defined by a single categorical factor, are all equal in the population.
need: To compare three or more independent group means without inflating the Type I error rate.
To analyse common experimental designs such as several diets, doses or treatments.
To partition total variability into a component explained by the factor and a residual (error) component.

classification.name: Between-groups variation
classification.text: Variation of group means around the grand mean, attributable to the factor being tested.

classification.name: Within-groups variation
classification.text: Variation of individual observations around their own group mean; treated as random error.

classification.name: Fixed-effects one-way ANOVA
classification.text: The groups compared are the specific levels of interest, as commonly used in this syllabus.

explanation: The null hypothesis is H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = … = μₖ; the alternative is that at least one group mean differs. Total variation (SST) is partitioned into between-groups (SSB) and within-groups (SSW) components: SST = SSB + SSW.

Each sum of squares is converted to a mean square by dividing by its degrees of freedom: MSB = SSB/(k−1) and MSW = SSW/(N−k), where k is the number of groups and N the total number of observations. The F statistic is F = MSB/MSW.

A large F indicates that between-group variation exceeds within-group (error) variation by more than chance alone would predict. If F is significant, ANOVA only shows that at least one mean differs; it does not identify which pairs differ. A planned post-hoc comparison, such as Tukey's HSD, is then needed and is treated here as a research-enrichment method beyond the core computational syllabus.

Assumptions are independent observations, approximately normal distribution of residuals within each group, and approximately equal population variances across groups (homogeneity of variance, which can be checked informally by comparing group SDs or with Levene's test as an enrichment method).

Zoology: Comparing mean growth of larvae reared under three or more independent diets.
Botany: Comparing mean plant height across several fertiliser treatments.
Biotechnology: Comparing expression levels across multiple independent culture conditions.
Microbiology: Comparing mean colony counts across several disinfectant concentrations.
Medicine: Comparing a clinical measurement across three or more treatment arms.
Agriculture: Comparing mean yield across several independent field treatments.
Fisheries: Comparing mean weight gain across three or more independent feed formulations.
Environmental science: Comparing a water-quality measure across several independent sampling sites.

advantages: Controls the overall Type I error rate when comparing several groups.
Uses all observations and partitions variability into interpretable components.
limitations: A significant F does not identify which specific groups differ.
Sensitive to marked departures from normality or equal variances, especially with unequal and small group sizes.
precautions: Confirm that groups are independent, not paired or repeated measures.
Check for at least approximate normality and comparable variances before relying on the standard F-test.
Plan post-hoc comparisons before, not only after, seeing a significant result.
Report F, both degrees of freedom, p-value and group means with SDs, not the F-value alone.

A larger F always means a biologically larger or more important effect.

title: Non-parametric Tests: Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank and Kruskal–Wallis
objectives: Explain when a non-parametric, rank-based test is preferable to its parametric counterpart.
Match the Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank and Kruskal–Wallis tests to the correct study design.

Interpret non-parametric results without overstating what they show.
intro: Parametric tests such as the t-test and ANOVA assume approximately normal data. When sample sizes are small and clearly skewed, contain influential outliers, or the outcome is only ordinal, rank-based non-parametric tests provide a robust alternative that does not depend on a specific distributional shape.
history: Frank Wilcoxon introduced rank-based tests for two-sample comparisons in 1945; Henry Mann and Donald Whitney developed an equivalent independent-samples test shortly afterwards, and William Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis extended the logic to more than two groups in 1952.
definition: Non-parametric tests evaluate hypotheses about distributions using the ranks of the data rather than the raw values and their assumed distributional form.
need: To analyse ordinal data that cannot legitimately be treated as interval or ratio.
To provide a robust alternative when normality is clearly violated and the sample is too small to rely on the Central Limit Theorem.
To reduce the influence of severe outliers, since ranking limits their leverage on the result.

classification.name: Mann–Whitney U test
classification.text: Non-parametric alternative to the independent-samples t-test, comparing two independent groups.

classification.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
classification.text: Non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test, using the ranked absolute differences within pairs.

classification.name: Kruskal–Wallis H test
classification.text: Non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA, comparing three or more independent groups.

explanation: The Mann–Whitney U test combines both independent samples, ranks all observations together, and compares the sum of ranks in each group. A large difference in rank sums, more than expected by chance, indicates the groups differ in location.

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test computes the difference for each pair, ranks the absolute differences, restores each rank's sign, and tests whether the signed-rank sum departs from zero more than chance would predict. Pairs with a difference of exactly zero are typically excluded before ranking.

The Kruskal–Wallis H test ranks all observations from every group together and compares the mean rank in each group, generalising the Mann–Whitney logic to three or more independent groups; a significant result, like ANOVA, requires a post-hoc procedure to locate which groups differ.

None of these three tests directly compares means; strictly they test for a difference in distribution or, under an assumption of similarly shaped distributions, a difference in medians. Tied ranks require a correction factor, usually applied automatically by statistical software.

Zoology: Comparing ordinal behavioural-intensity scores between two independent animal groups (Mann–Whitney).
Botany: Comparing skewed germination-time data before and after seed treatment (Wilcoxon signed-rank).
Biotechnology: Comparing small, non-normal expression datasets across three culture conditions (Kruskal–Wallis).
Microbiology: Comparing zone-of-inhibition data with a severe outlier between two disinfectants.
Medicine: Comparing symptom-severity ordinal scores between treatment and control groups.
Agriculture: Comparing non-normally distributed pest counts across several plots.
Fisheries: Comparing catch-per-unit-effort data with strong skew across sampling sites.
Environmental science: Comparing ranked pollution-severity categories between two rivers.

advantages: Do not require a normal distribution.
Robust to outliers because raw magnitudes are converted to ranks.
limitations: Generally less statistically powerful than the corresponding parametric test when normality genuinely holds.
Strictly test distributional or median differences rather than mean differences.
Large numbers of tied ranks require a correction and can complicate interpretation.
precautions: Do not choose a non-parametric test only because a parametric result was non-significant.
State clearly whether the design is independent or paired before selecting Mann–Whitney/Kruskal–Wallis or Wilcoxon.
Report median and interquartile range rather than mean and SD when using these tests.
Check whether an assumption of similarly shaped distributions is needed before interpreting a result as a median difference.

examples.q: Two independent, small samples of behavioural scores are clearly skewed. Which test compares them?
steps: Two independent groups → Mann–Whitney U rather than an independent t-test.
examples.answer: The Mann–Whitney U test.

examples.q: Germination times are measured for the same seed batch before and after a treatment. Which test is appropriate if the differences are skewed?
steps: Same experimental units measured twice → paired design.
Non-normal differences → Wilcoxon signed-rank rather than the paired t-test.
examples.answer: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

examples.q: Pest counts are compared across four independent plots and are strongly right-skewed. State the appropriate test and the reason a further step may be needed if it is significant.
steps: Four independent groups, non-normal → Kruskal–Wallis H test replaces one-way ANOVA.
A significant H indicates at least one group differs; a post-hoc rank-based comparison is then needed to locate which pairs differ.
examples.answer: Kruskal–Wallis H test, followed by an appropriate post-hoc procedure if H is significant.

misconceptions: Non-parametric tests require no assumptions whatsoever.
The Mann–Whitney U test always tests equality of means.
A non-parametric test should be used automatically whenever the sample is small.
exam: State the parametric counterpart of each non-parametric test.
Explain how ranking reduces the influence of outliers.
Give the correct design (independent or paired) for each test.
State what a significant result actually indicates about distributions or medians.
mnemonic: Two independent groups → Mann–Whitney; paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank; three or more independent groups → Kruskal–Wallis.
summary: Rank-based non-parametric tests provide robust alternatives to the t-test and ANOVA when normality is clearly violated.
Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon signed-rank and Kruskal–Wallis correspond respectively to the independent, paired and one-way ANOVA designs.
These tests trade some statistical power for robustness and fewer distributional assumptions.

title: Sample Size, Statistical Power and Study Design
objectives: Explain statistical power and its relationship to Type I and Type II error.
Identify the four factors that determine required sample size.
Calculate approximate sample size for estimating a mean or a proportion.
Discuss the ethical and practical importance of adequate sample-size planning.
intro: A study that is too small may fail to detect a real biological effect, wasting animals, materials and effort; a study that is unnecessarily large wastes resources and, in animal or clinical research, raises ethical concerns. Sample-size and power calculations should therefore be planned before data collection, not estimated afterwards.
history: The formal concept of statistical power was developed by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in the 1930s as part of their framework for hypothesis testing, complementing Fisher's earlier work on significance testing.
definition: Statistical power is the probability that a test correctly rejects a false null hypothesis; it is calculated as 1 minus the probability of a Type II error (1 − β).
need: To ensure a study has a reasonable chance of detecting a biologically meaningful effect if one exists.
To avoid wasting animals, reagents, time and cost on an underpowered or unnecessarily oversized study.
To justify sample size transparently in a project proposal, dissertation or ethics application.

classification.name: Type I error (α)
classification.text: Probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive); conventionally set at 0.05.

classification.name: Type II error (β)
classification.text: Probability of failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative).

classification.name: Statistical power (1−β)
classification.text: Probability of correctly detecting a real effect; commonly targeted at 0.80 or higher.

classification.name: Effect size
classification.text: The magnitude of the biological difference or association the study is designed to detect.

explanation: Four factors determine required sample size for a given test: the significance level α, the desired power (1−β), the expected effect size, and the variability (SD) of the outcome. Increasing the desired power or reducing the margin of error both increase the required sample size; a larger expected effect size or lower variability reduces it.

For estimating a population mean within a specified margin of error E, the approximate required sample size is n = (Z_{α/2}σ/E)². For estimating a population proportion, n = Z_{α/2}²p(1−p)/E², where p is an anticipated proportion (0.5 is used conservatively when p is unknown, since it maximises the required n).

Power calculations for comparing two means additionally require an estimate of the expected difference and its SD, typically taken from pilot data or previous literature; the underlying arithmetic corresponds to the sample size calculator used earlier in the Analysis Laboratory of this course.

Sample size and power planning are part of good experimental design, alongside replication, randomisation and appropriate controls; a well-powered but poorly designed study can still produce misleading results.

Zoology: Estimating how many animals are needed to detect a specified difference in growth between two diets.
Botany: Planning the number of plots needed to detect a stated yield difference with adequate power.
Biotechnology: Determining replicate number needed to detect a specified fold-change in expression.
Microbiology: Planning the number of plates needed to estimate a contamination rate within a stated margin.
Medicine: Justifying patient numbers in a clinical trial protocol and ethics submission.
Agriculture: Planning field-trial replication to detect a meaningful yield improvement.
Fisheries: Determining the number of fish to sample to estimate mean length within a stated precision.
Environmental science: Planning monitoring-station numbers to detect a specified change in a water-quality indicator.

advantages: Prevents wasted resources on studies too small to detect a meaningful effect.
Supports transparent, defensible research and ethics proposals.
limitations: Requires a credible prior estimate of variability or effect size, which is not always available.
Formulae here are approximate; complex designs need specialised software or a statistician.
precautions: Decide the desired effect size and power before data collection, not after seeing the results.
Do not increase sample size repeatedly until significance is reached (data peeking inflates the Type I error rate).
Use a conservative estimate of variability when uncertain.
Report the assumptions used in any sample-size justification.

examples.q: What does a statistical power of 0.80 mean?
examples.answer: There is an 80% chance of correctly detecting the specified real effect, and a 20% chance of missing it (Type II error).

examples.q: σ = 6, E = 2, Z_{α/2} = 1.96 (95% confidence). Estimate the required sample size for a mean.
examples.answer: Approximately 35 observations are required, rounding up.

examples.q: A pilot study suggests p ≈ 0.30 for an infection rate; a margin of error E = 0.05 at 95% confidence is required. Estimate n.
examples.answer: Approximately 323 observations are required, rounding up.

misconceptions: A larger sample size always guarantees a statistically significant result.
Power calculations are only needed for clinical trials, not for laboratory or field biology.
Increasing sample size after an initial non-significant result, without adjustment, is a valid way to ‘achieve’ significance.
confused: Type I error vs Type II error
Margin of error vs standard error
exam: Define Type I error, Type II error and power with a labelled diagram.
State the four factors that determine required sample size.
Show the sample-size formula for a mean and a proportion, with a worked substitution.
Explain why sample size should be planned before, not after, data collection.
mnemonic: Bigger effect, less variability, looser margin — smaller n; more power, tighter margin — larger n.
summary: Statistical power is the probability of correctly detecting a real effect and equals 1−β.
Required sample size depends on α, desired power, effect size and variability.
Sample-size planning should occur before data collection and be reported transparently.

formulae.name: Sample size for a mean
formulae.meaning: Approximate sample size to estimate a mean within margin of error E.

symbols.Z_{α/2}: critical value for the chosen confidence level

assumptions: Approximately normal sampling distribution of the mean
formulae.use: Planning sample size to estimate a mean with a stated precision.
formulae.avoid: Using an unrealistically small σ from an unrepresentative pilot.
formulae.bio: Planning how many fish to measure to estimate mean length within 2 cm.

formulae.name: Sample size for a proportion
formulae.meaning: Approximate sample size to estimate a proportion within margin of error E.

symbols.p: anticipated proportion (use 0.5 if unknown, for a conservative estimate)

formulae.use: Planning sample size to estimate a proportion, such as a prevalence or infection rate.
formulae.avoid: Ignoring finite-population correction for a small, fully accessible population.
formulae.bio: Planning how many animals to screen to estimate an infection rate within 5 percentage points.

formulae.meaning: Probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis.

symbols.β: probability of a Type II error

assumptions: A specific alternative (effect size) has been stated
formulae.use: Evaluating or planning a study's ability to detect a real effect.
formulae.avoid: Interpreting power without reference to a stated effect size.
formulae.bio: Probability that a growth trial detects a genuine feed-treatment difference.

title: Measures of Epidemiological Association: Relative Risk, Odds Ratio and Attributable Risk
objectives: Construct a 2×2 exposure–disease table and identify its four cells correctly.
Calculate and interpret relative risk, odds ratio and attributable risk.
Explain when relative risk versus odds ratio is the appropriate measure for a given study design.
Interpret these measures cautiously, distinguishing statistical association from causation.
intro: Chi-square testing (studied earlier) shows whether exposure and outcome are statistically associated in a contingency table, but it does not, by itself, express how much more likely the outcome is in the exposed group. Relative risk, odds ratio and attributable risk quantify the strength and public-health impact of an association.
history: These measures were formalised through twentieth-century epidemiological research, most famously in the British Doctors Study led by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill, which used relative risk to demonstrate the association between smoking and lung cancer.
definition: A 2×2 table cross-classifies exposure status (exposed/unexposed) against outcome status (disease/no disease). Relative risk (RR) compares the risk of disease between exposed and unexposed groups; the odds ratio (OR) compares the odds of exposure between diseased and non-diseased groups; attributable risk (AR) is the absolute risk difference.
need: To quantify how much more (or less) likely an outcome is in an exposed group than an unexposed group.
To support public-health and clinical decisions about the practical impact of an exposure.
To choose the correct summary measure for cohort versus case-control study designs.

classification.name: Relative risk (risk ratio)
classification.text: Ratio of the risk of disease in the exposed group to the risk in the unexposed group; appropriate for cohort and experimental designs where incidence can be measured directly.

classification.name: Odds ratio
classification.text: Ratio of the odds of exposure among diseased individuals to the odds among non-diseased individuals; the standard measure for case-control studies, where incidence cannot be calculated directly.

classification.name: Attributable risk (risk difference)
classification.text: Absolute difference between the risk in the exposed group and the risk in the unexposed group; expresses the excess risk due to exposure.

explanation: In a standard 2×2 table with cells a (exposed, diseased), b (exposed, not diseased), c (unexposed, diseased) and d (unexposed, not diseased): risk in the exposed group = a/(a+b); risk in the unexposed group = c/(c+d). RR = [a/(a+b)] ÷ [c/(c+d)].

The odds ratio is calculated as OR = (a×d)/(b×c), the cross-product ratio. In a case-control design, where subjects are sampled by outcome status rather than followed forward in time, individual risks cannot be calculated directly, so the odds ratio is used instead of relative risk; when the disease is rare, OR approximates RR reasonably well.

Attributable risk, AR = risk_exposed − risk_unexposed, is expressed in the original risk units and estimates the excess disease burden directly attributable to the exposure; unlike RR and OR, it depends on the baseline risk of the population and cannot simply be transferred to a population with a very different baseline rate.

A value of 1 for RR or OR indicates no association; values above 1 indicate increased risk or odds with exposure, and values below 1 indicate a protective association. As with chi-square, an association shown by these measures does not by itself establish causation; study design, confounding and bias must always be considered.

Zoology: Comparing disease risk between wild-caught and captive-bred animal cohorts.
Botany: Comparing the risk of fungal infection between treated and untreated plant plots.
Biotechnology: Comparing contamination odds between two culture-handling protocols in a case-control style audit.
Microbiology: Comparing the risk of resistant-strain isolation between two antibiotic-exposure groups.
Medicine: Comparing disease risk between exposed and unexposed patient cohorts, and exposure odds in case-control studies.
Agriculture: Comparing crop-failure risk between two irrigation practices.
Fisheries: Comparing mortality risk between two stocking densities.
Environmental science: Comparing the risk of a health outcome between populations near and away from a pollution source.

advantages: Provide an intuitive, quantified measure of association beyond a bare significance test.
Attributable risk expresses public-health impact in directly interpretable absolute terms.
limitations: The odds ratio can overstate the relative risk when the outcome is common rather than rare.
All three measures are vulnerable to confounding and selection bias unless the study is carefully designed.
Attributable risk from one population cannot be transferred uncritically to a population with a different baseline risk.
precautions: Confirm the study design (cohort/experimental versus case-control) before choosing RR or OR.
Label the 2×2 table cells (a, b, c, d) clearly and consistently before calculating.
Report a confidence interval alongside RR, OR or AR wherever possible, not a bare point estimate.
Avoid causal language when the design cannot support a causal conclusion.

examples.q: In a 2×2 table, a=30, b=70, c=15, d=85. Calculate the risk of disease in the exposed group.
examples.answer: Risk in the exposed group = 0.30 (30%).

examples.q: Using the same table (a=30, b=70, c=15, d=85), calculate the relative risk.
examples.answer: RR = 2.0; exposed individuals have twice the risk of the unexposed group.

examples.q: For a=30, b=70, c=15, d=85, calculate the odds ratio and the attributable risk, and comment on which measure is used for a case-control design.
steps: A case-control study cannot compute risks directly, so OR (≈2.43) rather than RR would be reported.
examples.answer: OR ≈ 2.43; AR = 0.15 (15 percentage points); a case-control study would report the odds ratio.

misconceptions: Relative risk and odds ratio always give numerically identical results.
A relative risk greater than 1 proves that the exposure causes the disease.
Attributable risk can be applied unchanged to any population regardless of its baseline risk.
exam: Draw and label a standard 2×2 exposure–disease table.
Give the RR, OR and AR formulae with clear symbol definitions.
Explain why OR rather than RR is used in case-control studies.
Discuss confounding as a threat to causal interpretation of these measures.
mnemonic: RR compares risks; OR compares odds; AR is the risk difference (excess risk).
summary: A 2×2 table cross-classifies exposure against outcome and underlies RR, OR and AR.
RR suits cohort/experimental designs; OR is the standard measure for case-control designs and approximates RR when disease is rare.
Attributable risk expresses the absolute excess risk due to exposure but is population-specific.

formulae.name: Relative risk
formulae.meaning: Ratio of risk in the exposed group to risk in the unexposed group.
assumptions: Cohort or experimental design where incidence can be measured directly
formulae.use: Comparing disease risk between exposed and unexposed groups.
formulae.avoid: Case-control designs, where incidence cannot be directly calculated.
formulae.bio: Comparing infection risk between treated and untreated animal cohorts.

formulae.name: Odds ratio
formulae.meaning: Ratio of the odds of exposure among diseased individuals to the odds among non-diseased individuals.

symbols.a,b,c,d: 2×2 table cell counts as defined for relative risk

assumptions: Valid for any 2×2 design; the standard measure for case-control studies
formulae.use: Case-control studies, or as an approximation to RR when disease is rare.
formulae.avoid: Presenting OR as if it were RR when the outcome is common.
formulae.bio: Comparing exposure odds between diseased and disease-free sampled animals.

formulae.name: Attributable risk
formulae.meaning: Absolute excess risk in the exposed group compared with the unexposed group.
assumptions: Cohort or experimental design with directly measured risks
formulae.use: Quantifying the absolute public-health impact of an exposure.
formulae.avoid: Transferring the value unchanged to a population with a different baseline risk.
formulae.bio: Excess disease risk attributable to a specific husbandry practice.

Why doesn't a significant association prove causation?

title: Statistical and Office Software for Data Analysis: Excel, SPSS and R
objectives: Compare Excel, SPSS and R as tools for statistical data analysis in biological research.
Identify which software is best suited to a given task, dataset size and reproducibility need.
Explain good practice for organising data before analysis in any of these tools.
Describe how to verify software output against hand calculation for teaching purposes.
intro: Every calculation practised in this course, from a mean to an ANOVA, can be produced by dedicated software far faster than by hand. Choosing the right tool, and using it correctly, is itself a practical skill expected of a biology graduate working with data.
history: Spreadsheets such as Excel became widespread from the 1980s; SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences) was developed from the late 1960s for menu-driven statistical analysis; R, a free and open-source language for statistical computing, was released in the 1990s and has since become widely used in academic research.
definition: Statistical software refers to applications used to organise, analyse, visualise and report data. Excel is a general-purpose spreadsheet with statistical functions and add-ins; SPSS is a menu-driven dedicated statistical package; R is a free, open-source scripting language and environment for statistical computing.
need: To perform calculations accurately and quickly on datasets too large for convenient hand calculation.
To produce publication-quality tables, charts and statistical output.
To support reproducibility, since scripted or logged analysis can be checked and repeated exactly.

classification.name: Excel
classification.text: Spreadsheet software with built-in statistical functions (e.g. AVERAGE, STDEV, CORREL) and an optional Data Analysis ToolPak for t-tests, ANOVA, regression and descriptive statistics.

classification.name: SPSS
classification.text: Menu-driven dedicated statistical package widely used in the social, health and life sciences, organising data in a Data View and variable metadata in a Variable View.

classification.name: R (with RStudio)
classification.text: Free, open-source scripting language and environment, extended by thousands of packages, favoured for reproducible and advanced statistical analysis.

explanation: Excel is widely available and familiar, and it is adequate for descriptive statistics, simple charts and small datasets, but repeated manual steps are more error-prone and less reproducible than a saved script or logged procedure, and its statistical output can be less complete than dedicated packages for advanced tests.

SPSS provides menu-driven analysis through an Analyze menu, with results delivered in a separate Output Viewer; it is well suited to standard tests such as t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square and regression without requiring programming, but it is proprietary licensed software.

R requires learning simple scripting syntax, but a saved R script provides an exact, repeatable and freely shareable record of every analysis step; it is free, extensible through packages for almost any statistical method, and increasingly expected in graduate-level research.

Whichever tool is used, the underlying statistical logic taught throughout this course, hypotheses, assumptions, degrees of freedom and correct interpretation, does not change; software automates calculation, not statistical judgement. New users should first reproduce a small worked example from earlier lessons by hand and then confirm that the software gives the same result, before trusting it on real data.

Zoology: Using Excel for a quick descriptive summary of a small class field dataset.
Botany: Using SPSS to run an independent-samples t-test comparing two treatment groups.
Biotechnology: Using R to script a reproducible ANOVA and post-hoc analysis across several culture conditions.
Microbiology: Using Excel charts to present colony-count trends for a laboratory report.
Medicine: Using SPSS to analyse clinical trial data with standard menu-driven procedures.
Agriculture: Using R to analyse multi-site field-trial data reproducibly across seasons.
Fisheries: Using Excel's Data Analysis ToolPak for a quick regression on length–weight data.
Environmental science: Using R scripts to reanalyse long-term monitoring data as new data arrive.

advantages: Dedicated software performs calculations far faster and with fewer arithmetic errors than manual computation on large datasets.
A saved script or logged procedure supports reproducibility and peer verification.
limitations: Software cannot compensate for an inappropriate test choice, poor data quality or violated assumptions.
Licensing cost may restrict access to SPSS and similar proprietary packages outside institutional access.
Menu-driven output can be misread or misreported if the underlying statistics are not understood.
precautions: Keep an unedited copy of the raw dataset separate from any working or cleaned file.
Verify software output against a small hand-calculated example before trusting it on a full dataset.
Record and save the exact steps, menu choices or script used, so the analysis can be checked or repeated.
Check that the software's default test matches the assumptions actually satisfied by the data.

examples.q: Which Excel function calculates the arithmetic mean of a data range?
steps: Excel provides a dedicated built-in statistical function for the mean.
examples.answer: =AVERAGE(range)

examples.q: A researcher needs a fully reproducible, freely shareable analysis script for a multi-site dataset that will be reanalysed each season. Which tool is generally best suited?
steps: Reproducibility and free, exact repeatability across seasons favour a scripted language.
R scripts can be saved, shared and rerun exactly.
examples.answer: R is generally best suited for this reproducible, repeated-analysis requirement.

examples.q: Explain the verification step a student should perform before trusting a new statistical software package for coursework.
steps: Take a small dataset already solved by hand earlier in the course, such as a one-sample t-test.
Enter the same data into the software.
Compare the software's t, df and p with the hand-calculated values.
Only proceed to larger, unseen datasets once the two match.
examples.answer: Verifying software output against a known hand-calculated result builds justified confidence before relying on the software for coursework or research.

misconceptions: Any statistical software automatically selects the correct test for the data.
A p-value produced by software is trustworthy regardless of whether test assumptions were checked.
R is only for advanced programmers and has no place in undergraduate biology.
SPSS and Excel always give identical numerical output for the same test.
confused: Data View vs Variable View in SPSS
Free/open-source software vs proprietary licensed software

Describe the general workflow for running a t-test in a menu-driven package.
Explain why a saved script improves reproducibility compared with manual menu clicks.
State the verification step recommended before trusting new software.
mnemonic: Excel for quick and familiar; SPSS for menu-driven standard tests; R for scripted, reproducible and advanced analysis.
summary: Excel, SPSS and R each suit different needs of cost, ease of use, dataset size and reproducibility.
Software automates calculation but does not replace correct test selection, assumption checking or interpretation.
New users should verify software output against a hand-calculated example before relying on it for coursework or research.
